Question three. What is a consumer group, and how does it scale consumption? A consumer group is a set of consumers that read one topic together. Each partition goes to exactly one of them, so the work is split and nothing is read twice. Two consumers share three partitions. Add a third, and the group rebalances: one partition each. Add a fourth, and it sits idle. Parallelism stops at the partition count. A second group gets every message again, on its own: that's how one stream feeds several pipelines. Question four. What are consumer offsets and why commit them? A commit records how far the group has processed each partition, and Kafka stores it. After a crash or a rebalance, the next owner resumes from the last commit, not from the start. So when you commit decides what a crash costs.

Question five. What is the difference between at-least-once, at-most-once, and exactly-once? Take one batch, offsets five to nine, and a crash just after seven. Commit first, then process, and eight and nine are skipped for good. That's at-most-once: no duplicates, but messages lost. Process first, then commit, and after the crash, five to seven run again. That's at-least-once: nothing lost, but duplicates. It's the usual default, though it can't save a message deleted before anyone read it. Exactly-once means each message has one effect on the result. Not that the code runs once: it can run twice, as long as the second run changes nothing. Model it: a thousand messages, committed every fifty, with three crashes. At-most-once loses fifty-four. At-least-once processes ninety-six of them twice.
